pr_body:
Fix #4593. With colors where `min` and `mid` resolve to the same value, such as `#ff8080`, the `set_sat()` function would pick a reference to the same channel twice when selecting `min`, `max` and `mid`, so I tweaked the logic to account for this edge case.

I did this with inline functions because the linter doesn't seem to like nested ternaries, but both ways should compile to the same thing.

Side note: I'm leaving the comment on top of `set_sat()` as I'm not sure if the way saturation is being set is correct either, though the results *look* just about right to me. I tried a few alternate formulas to check this, but they were much more computationally expensive, and the difference was not very noticeable, so in the end I just left the calculation untouched.
pr_comments: It works great! With this patch we offer a result similar to Affinity Photo: https://github.com/aseprite/aseprite/issues/4593#issuecomment-2681962770

issue_context.title: Saturation blend mode on hue 0
issue_context.body:
When using a color with hue 0, the Saturation blend mode doesn't correctly set the saturation value of said color

How to recreate:
Use a color with a hue of 0, for instance #ff8080 seems to work well.
In a layer above, overlap the red color with another (or even the same) color and set the blend mode of that layer to Saturation.

review_comments:
I had to use pointers instead of references for the ordering to work, but it's working nicely. If rewriting the function to use pointers is no problem, then I'd go with this one for readability.

To briefly touch on performance: it varies from platform to platform. This alternative is likely the more performant approach on x86_64 when compiling with clang; glancing at the disassembly I'm seeing that it's generating much better code (branchless and around half as many instructions), but for other platforms I couldn't tell.

I'll be testing the solution of this PR as it is in e359cb70105fa05da7bbf1af28445f5f447a1851 and trying to merge it.

In case someone wants to compare performance of different solutions, `src/doc/blend_benchmark.cpp` is a good place to start.
